About the same time (we're still doing a bunch of benchmarks, but so far it looks like nothing changes) How do you achieve that given the sync becomes much more complicated w/ beacon chain docked? It does not (it actually becomes easier) The beacon node will give us a (fairly) recent header. We will reverse header sync with that (download the header chain from this down to genesis), then we download the blocks and the state at the recent header. If the beacon chain advances and gives us another header, we will integrate it into our sync. Hopefully I can start to make meaningful contributions in the near future :) How do you know that a certain header's state root is a valid one? we don't know with snap sync until we downloaded all state, this is the weakened assumption that you get with snap sync vs full sync But don't we know if the state root is valid on PoW? No As we can verify PoW proofs without looking at anything else But with PoS the consensus is "contextual" We don't know until we have the state I think you might be misunderstanding my question You can verify the PoW, but that only tells you that a certain amount of hashrate has been used to produce a block, it tells us nothing about the state root nor the total amount of hashrate on the network With PoW, you can verify all headers of the canonical chain without knowing anything about the chain state, and then get the latest 64-block deep state root and then proceed with fast/snap sync. But with PoS, don't you have to have the synced beacon chain access to verify that a certain proof of stake is correct? Yeah you misunderstood this Please check out this one Yes, the beacon chain has to optimistically sync from the recent checkpoint onwards until the EL catches up and we can fully verify everything. But it doesn't make syncing that much slower What does optimistically mean? You have to ask the CL devs about that^^ Hah ok Perhaps trusting the 66% of validators? It's just about postponing validation of the execution payload afaik, while the EL client catches up. It's similar to validating PoW proofs and headers without validating the transaction payload I guess, but then in a PoS world. I don't think it's necessary to have a synced up beacon chain (you can be behind). Similar to snap/fast sync for the EL side, there is "checkpoint sync" for CL clients to quickly sync to a trusted point (which takes a minute or two). Then they will in the background backfill history, while staying in sync with the network. Contrary to snap sync though, you have to _provide_ this trusted point yourself (e.g. a link to a REST endpoint, or a file you got from a friend). excerpts.author: alexssd7fp

excerpts.author: mariusvanderwijden
excerpts.content:
It does not (it actually becomes easier)
The beacon node will give us a (fairly) recent header. We will reverse header sync with that (download the header chain from this down to genesis), then we download the blocks and the state at the recent header. If the beacon chain advances and gives us another header, we will integrate it into our sync. The big time wastes are in downloading the blocks and the state, which are the same pre and post merge

excerpts.author: pietjepuk

excerpts.author: pietjepuk
excerpts.content: It's similar to validating PoW proofs and headers without validating the transaction payload I guess, but then in a PoS world.

excerpts.author: pietjepuk
excerpts.content:
I don't think it's necessary to have a synced up beacon chain (you can be behind). Similar to snap/fast sync for the EL side, there is "checkpoint sync" for CL clients to quickly sync to a trusted point (which takes a minute or two). Then they will in the background backfill history, while staying in sync with the network. 
Contrary to snap sync though, you have to _provide_ this trusted point yourself (e.g. a link to a REST endpoint, or a file you got from a friend).
